Diabetes Care 2006; 29: 1458–9. Hyperparathyroidism. Vitamin D has been used for certain forms of hyperparathyroidism (p.1087). The secondary hyper- parathyroidism of renal osteodystrophy (p.1086) may respond to treatment with calcitriol, or its analogue alfacalcidol,1,2 which do not require renal hydroxylation for activation. Calcitriol has been used orally,3 intravenously,3,4 and intraperitoneally;5 percu- taneous injection directly into the parathyroid gland has also been reported to be safe and effective.6-8 However, doses capable of suppressing parathyroid hormone secretion may lead to hy- percalcaemia,1-3,5,9,10 hyperphosphataemia,1,2,5,9,10 and a decline in renal function;11 the increase in calcium and phosphate may promote soft tissue and vascular calcification,1,2 see Hypercal- caemia, under Adverse Effects, above. Newer analogues for this indication include paricalcitol,12-15 doxercalciferol,16-18 falecalcitriol,19 and maxacalcitol.20-25 These are reported to have less effect on calcium and phosphate con- centrations, while retaining the suppressive effect on parathyroid hormone;1,5,9,10 however, some2,18 consider clinically relevant benefit to be lacking.
